nodes.label: Agenda 21
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Non-binding action plan of UN adopted at Rio Earth Summit 1992. Aims at global sustainable development. Addresses poverty, environmental protection, resource management. India is a signatory.

nodes.label: Global Warming
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Long-term increase in Earth's average surface temperature due to enhanced greenhouse effect from anthropogenic emissions. CO2 levels risen from 280 ppm (pre-industrial) to over 420 ppm. Causes sea-level rise, melting glaciers, extreme weather events, and ecosystem disruption. Paris Agreement aims to limit warming to 1.5-2C.
nodes.chapter_title: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature

nodes.label: Sustainable Resource Development
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Rio Earth Summit 1992 (Agenda 21) emphasized sustainable development. Brundtland Commission defined it: development meeting present needs without compromising future generations. India committed to sustainable development goals.

nodes.label: India's Forest Cover
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Forest cover about 24.56% of total area (2019 FSI). Reserved forests (over 50%), protected forests, unclassed forests. Dense forests decreasing, open forests increasing. Target is 33%.

nodes.label: India's Flora and Fauna Diversity
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: About 47000 plant species (1200 endemic). 89000+ animal species. Over 12% of world's recorded birds. India is one of 12 mega-biodiversity countries. Many species still being discovered.

nodes.label: IUCN Categories
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Normal, endangered, vulnerable, rare, endemic, extinct. About 10% plants and 20% mammals in India are on threatened list. 1300 plant species and 20+ animal species in endangered category.

nodes.label: Causes of Forest Depletion
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Colonial exploitation for timber, railway sleepers, ship-building. Post-independence: agricultural expansion, mining, river valley projects, infrastructure development. Large-scale grazing and fuel wood collection.

nodes.label: Indian Wildlife Protection Act 1972
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Comprehensive legislation for wildlife protection. Provides for national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves. Bans hunting. Lists protected species in schedules. Amended several times since.

nodes.label: Biodiversity Hotspots of India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Western Ghats and NE India are among global biodiversity hotspots. Western Ghats have 4000+ endemic plant species. NE India part of Indo-Burma hotspot. High species diversity but threatened by habitat loss.

nodes.label: Traditional Water Harvesting
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Ancient systems: stepwells/vavs (Gujarat), talabs/ahars (UP/Bihar), eris (Tamil Nadu), surangams (Kerala), kattas (Karnataka). Built over centuries, community-managed. Many being revived for water conservation.

nodes.label: Bamboo Drip Irrigation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Traditional system in Meghalaya using bamboo pipes to tap stream water for irrigation. 200-year-old system. About 18-20 litres of water enters bamboo network and reduces to 20-80 drops per minute at plant base.

nodes.label: Coal in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Primary energy source, 67% of commercial energy. Two types: Gondwana (98% of reserves, Damodar valley, Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro) and Tertiary (NE states, Jammu, Rajasthan, poor quality). India 3rd largest producer.

nodes.label: Petroleum in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Occurs in fault traps of sedimentary rocks. Major fields: Mumbai High (63% of production), Gujarat, Assam (oldest field Digboi). Krishna-Godavari and Kaveri basins. India imports over 80% of oil needs.

nodes.label: India's Non-Conventional Energy
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Solar: huge potential, 300 clear sunny days. Wind: 5th largest installed capacity, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Rajasthan. Nuclear: Rawatbhata, Tarapur, Kalpakkam, Narora, Kaiga. Biogas: 12 million plants. Geothermal: Manikaran, Puga Valley.

nodes.label: Thermal Power in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Uses coal, petroleum, natural gas. Generates about 65% of India's electricity. Major stations near coal fields. Pollution concerns. Government promoting shift to cleaner energy.

nodes.label: India's Solar Energy Potential
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India receives about 300 clear sunny days annually, especially in Rajasthan, Gujarat, TN. National Solar Mission targets 100 GW by 2022. Solar parks in Rajasthan and Gujarat. Bhadla Solar Park world's largest.

nodes.label: India's Wind Energy
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 5th largest installed capacity globally. Major farms in Tamil Nadu (largest), Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh. Jaisalmer cluster among largest. India aims 60 GW by 2022.

nodes.label: Konkan Railway
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 720 km railway along western coast from Roha to Mangalore. Engineering marvel with 2000 bridges and 91 tunnels through Western Ghats. Completed in 1998. Connects Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka.

nodes.label: Tourism Industry in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Growing industry contributing 6.23% to GDP. 15.24 million foreign arrivals (2019). Heritage, medical, adventure, eco-tourism. Incredible India campaign. Foreign exchange earner, employment generator.

nodes.label: Differentiation of Earth
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Process by which the early homogeneous earth separated into concentric layers of different density. Heavy materials like iron and nickel sank to form the core, while lighter silicates floated up to form the mantle and crust. Driven by heat from radioactive decay and gravitational compression.
nodes.chapter_title: Origin and Evolution of the Earth

nodes.label: Degassing
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Release of gases from the earth's interior through volcanic activity during early earth history. Produced the primitive atmosphere rich in water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, and ammonia but lacking free oxygen. Led to the formation of the early atmosphere and oceans.
nodes.chapter_title: Origin and Evolution of the Earth

nodes.label: Origin of Atmosphere
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Earth's early atmosphere formed through degassing of the interior. First atmosphere was hydrogen and helium-rich but was lost to solar winds. Second atmosphere from volcanic gases lacked free oxygen. Free oxygen appeared only after photosynthetic organisms evolved about 2.5 billion years ago.
nodes.chapter_title: Origin and Evolution of the Earth

nodes.label: Origin of Oceans
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Oceans formed when the earth cooled enough for water vapour in the atmosphere to condense and fall as rain. This accumulated in low-lying areas over millions of years. Occurred approximately 3.8 billion years ago. Some water may also have come from cometary impacts.
nodes.chapter_title: Origin and Evolution of the Earth

nodes.label: Origin of Life
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Life originated about 3.8 billion years ago in the oceans. Chemical evolution of organic molecules preceded biological evolution. First organisms were unicellular prokaryotes. Photosynthesis by cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) oxygenated the atmosphere, enabling complex life.
nodes.chapter_title: Origin and Evolution of the Earth

nodes.label: Moon Formation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: The giant impact hypothesis suggests the moon formed when a Mars-sized body (Theia) collided with the proto-Earth about 4.5 billion years ago. Debris from the collision accreted to form the moon. Explains the moon's lower density and similar isotopic composition to Earth.
nodes.chapter_title: Origin and Evolution of the Earth

nodes.label: Earthquake
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Sudden release of energy in the earth's lithosphere causing seismic waves. Caused by tectonic plate movements, volcanic activity, or faulting. Focus (hypocenter) is the point of origin inside earth. Epicenter is the point on surface directly above focus. Most occur along plate boundaries.

nodes.label: Volcano
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Opening in earth's surface through which magma, gases, and pyroclastic material erupt. Types include shield volcanoes (basaltic, gentle slopes), composite/stratovolcanoes (violent eruptions), and cinder cones. Products include lava, ash, pyroclastic debris, and volcanic gases including sulphur and nitrogen compounds.

nodes.label: Volcanic Landforms
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Landforms created by volcanic activity. Intrusive forms include batholiths (large deep bodies), laccoliths (dome-shaped), dykes (vertical sheets), sills (horizontal sheets), and lopoliths (saucer-shaped). Extrusive forms include volcanic cones, craters, calderas, and lava plateaus like Deccan Traps.

nodes.label: Batholith
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Large body of intrusive igneous rock formed deep underground when magma cools slowly. Covers areas of 100+ sq km. Made of coarse-grained granite. Exposed at surface after erosion of overlying rock. Examples include the Idaho batholith and the coastal batholith of Peru.

nodes.label: Laccolith
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Dome-shaped intrusive igneous body that has pushed up overlying strata. Has a flat floor and convex upper surface. Formed when viscous magma intrudes between rock layers but cannot spread horizontally. Karnataka Plateau has examples of exposed laccoliths.

nodes.label: Endogenic Forces
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Internal forces originating from within the earth driven by geothermal energy and radioactive heat. Include diastrophism (folding, faulting) and volcanism. Responsible for building up landforms - mountains, plateaus, rifts. Operate suddenly (earthquakes) or slowly (continental drift, mountain building).

nodes.label: Exogenic Forces
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: External forces driven by solar energy acting on the earth's surface. Include weathering, mass wasting, erosion, and deposition. Work to level down the landforms created by endogenic forces. Agents include water, wind, glaciers, and waves. Climate determines which agent dominates in a region.

nodes.label: Weathering
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: In-situ mechanical disintegration and chemical decomposition of rocks at or near the earth's surface. No transportation involved (distinguishes from erosion). Three types: physical/mechanical, chemical, and biological. Climate is the key factor - chemical weathering dominates in hot humid areas, physical in arid and cold areas.

nodes.label: Physical Weathering
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Mechanical disintegration of rocks without chemical change. Processes include frost wedging (water freezes in cracks and expands), thermal expansion and contraction (exfoliation), salt crystallization, and pressure release (unloading). Dominant in arid, semi-arid, and cold regions. Produces angular rock fragments.

nodes.label: Chemical Weathering
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Decomposition of rocks through chemical reactions. Processes include oxidation (iron minerals rust), carbonation (CO2 dissolves limestone), hydration (minerals absorb water and expand), and solution. Rainfall containing dissolved CO2 forms weak carbonic acid that dissolves calcite. Dominant in hot, humid climates.

nodes.label: Biological Weathering
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Weathering caused by living organisms. Plant roots grow into cracks and widen them. Burrowing animals (earthworms, rodents) loosen soil. Lichens and mosses produce acids that decompose rock surfaces. Humans accelerate weathering through mining, construction, and deforestation.

nodes.label: Erosion
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Removal and transportation of weathered material by natural agents. Agents include running water (rivers), wind, glaciers, waves, and groundwater. Different from weathering as it involves movement. Soil erosion sequence: splash erosion, sheet erosion, rill erosion, gully erosion. Climate and vegetation cover are key factors.

nodes.label: Mass Wasting/Mass Movement
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Downslope movement of weathered material under gravity without a transporting agent. Types include creep (very slow), solifluction (in permafrost areas), landslides (rapid), mudflows, rockfalls, and avalanches. Triggered by heavy rainfall, earthquakes, or slope undercutting. More common on steep slopes with loose material.

nodes.label: Deposition
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Process by which eroded material is laid down when the transporting agent loses energy. Creates depositional landforms like deltas, alluvial plains, sand dunes, moraines, and beaches. Occurs when velocity or competence of the agent decreases. Builds up low-lying areas and creates fertile plains.

nodes.label: Diastrophism
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Deformation of the earth's crust by tectonic forces. Includes epeirogenic (vertical, continent-building) and orogenic (horizontal, mountain-building) movements. Produces folds, faults, joints, and fractures. Responsible for creating major relief features like mountains, plateaus, and rift valleys.

nodes.label: Folding
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Bending of rock layers due to compressive forces. Creates anticlines (upfolds) and synclines (downfolds). Types include symmetrical, asymmetrical, overturned, recumbent, and isoclinal folds. Fold mountains (Himalayas, Alps, Andes, Rockies) are formed by intense folding of sedimentary layers at convergent plate boundaries.

nodes.label: Faulting
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Fracturing of rock with displacement along the fracture plane. Types include normal fault (tensional forces), reverse fault (compressional), strike-slip/transform fault (lateral movement). Creates horsts (uplifted blocks) and grabens (down-dropped blocks). Rift valleys are formed by block faulting.

nodes.label: Soil Formation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Process of developing soil from parent rock through weathering and addition of organic matter. Five soil-forming factors: parent material, climate, organisms, topography, and time (CLORPT). Weathering breaks rock into regolith, biological processes add humus. Soil profile develops with O, A, B, C horizons over time.

nodes.label: Soil Erosion
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Removal of topsoil by wind, water, or ice faster than it can be replenished. Sequence: splash erosion, sheet erosion, rill erosion, gully erosion. Accelerated by deforestation, overgrazing, and improper farming. Conservation methods include contour ploughing, terracing, strip cropping, windbreaks, and crop rotation.

nodes.label: Exfoliation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Physical weathering process where outer layers of rock peel off in concentric sheets due to thermal expansion-contraction cycles or pressure release. Common in hot deserts where large diurnal temperature range causes repeated expansion and contraction. Creates rounded landforms like tors and inselbergs.

nodes.label: Carbonation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Chemical weathering process where carbon dioxide dissolved in rainwater forms weak carbonic acid (H2CO3) that reacts with calcium carbonate in limestone. Produces soluble calcium bicarbonate that is carried away in solution. Responsible for formation of karst landforms - caves, sinkholes, stalactites, stalagmites.

nodes.label: Oxidation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Chemical weathering process where oxygen combines with minerals in rocks, particularly iron-bearing minerals. Iron reacts with oxygen and water to form iron oxide (rust), causing rocks to crumble and turn reddish-brown. Common in humid climates. Laterite soils are a product of intense oxidation in tropical areas.

nodes.label: Delta
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Triangular depositional landform at the mouth of a river where it enters a sea or lake. Formed when the river's sediment load exceeds the capacity of the sea to remove it. Types include arcuate (Nile, Ganga), bird-foot (Mississippi), and cuspate (Tiber). Extremely fertile due to alluvial soil.

nodes.label: Floodplain
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Flat area adjacent to a river channel that is periodically flooded. Formed by deposition of alluvium during floods. Features natural levees (raised banks) and backswamps. Extremely fertile agricultural land. Major floodplains include the Indo-Gangetic plain and Nile valley.

nodes.label: Alluvial Fan
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Fan-shaped depositional feature formed where a river emerges from mountains onto a plain. Sudden decrease in gradient causes the river to deposit its sediment load. Coarser material near apex, finer material at the edges. Common at the foothills of the Himalayas. Larger versions called alluvial cones.

nodes.label: Karst Landforms
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Landforms developed in soluble rocks like limestone by solution action of groundwater. Includes sinkholes (dolines), caves, caverns, stalactites (hanging from ceiling), stalagmites (rising from floor), pillars, disappearing streams, and uvalas. Named after the Karst region in Slovenia. Cherrapunji in Meghalaya has karst features.

nodes.label: Stalactite and Stalagmite
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Cave formations (speleothems) in limestone caves. Stalactites hang from the ceiling like icicles, formed by dripping water depositing calcium carbonate. Stalagmites grow upward from the cave floor from the same dripping process. When they join, they form a pillar or column. Process is very slow.

nodes.label: Carbon Dioxide
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Greenhouse gas present at about 0.04% (420+ ppm and rising). Transparent to incoming solar radiation but absorbs outgoing infrared radiation, causing the greenhouse effect. Increasing due to fossil fuel burning and deforestation. Essential for photosynthesis. Rising levels are the primary driver of global warming.

nodes.label: Greenhouse Effect
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Natural process where certain atmospheric gases trap outgoing infrared radiation and re-radiate it back to earth, keeping the planet warm enough (average 15C) to support life. Without it, earth's average temperature would be about -18C. Enhanced greenhouse effect from human emissions is causing global warming.

nodes.label: Terrestrial Radiation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Long-wave infrared radiation emitted by the earth's surface after absorbing solar radiation. Earth radiates energy as heat, which is absorbed by greenhouse gases and re-radiated. This is the mechanism of the greenhouse effect. Net outgoing radiation is balanced by incoming solar radiation over long periods.
nodes.chapter_title: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature

nodes.label: Earth's Heat Budget
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Balance between incoming solar radiation and outgoing terrestrial radiation. Of 100 units of incoming solar energy: 35 reflected (albedo), 14 absorbed by atmosphere, 51 absorbed by earth's surface. Earth re-radiates 51 units as long-wave radiation. Overall, incoming equals outgoing maintaining thermal equilibrium globally, though not at all latitudes.
nodes.chapter_title: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature

nodes.label: Albedo
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Fraction of solar radiation reflected back by a surface. Earth's average albedo is about 30-35%. Fresh snow has the highest albedo (80-90%), while dark ocean surfaces have the lowest (6-10%). Forests, deserts, and clouds have varying albedo. Changes in ice cover affect albedo and thus climate (ice-albedo feedback).
nodes.chapter_title: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature

nodes.label: Tropical Cyclone
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Intense low-pressure system forming over warm tropical oceans (SST above 27C). Called hurricanes (Atlantic), typhoons (Pacific), cyclones (Indian Ocean). Features calm eye at center surrounded by eye wall with strongest winds. Fueled by latent heat from warm ocean water. Weakens over land. Coriolis force needed for rotation.

nodes.label: Monsoon Winds
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Seasonal reversal of wind direction caused by differential heating of land and ocean. Summer monsoon: winds blow from ocean to land bringing heavy rainfall. Winter monsoon: winds blow from land to ocean, generally dry. Most pronounced in South and Southeast Asia. ITCZ shift over the Indian subcontinent drives the Indian monsoon.

nodes.label: Condensation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Process by which water vapour changes to liquid water when air is cooled to its dew point. Requires condensation nuclei (dust, salt, pollen particles). Forms dew, frost, fog, mist, and clouds depending on where it occurs. Essential step between evaporation and precipitation in the water cycle.

nodes.label: Precipitation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Water falling from clouds to the earth's surface in any form - rain, snow, sleet, hail. Occurs when cloud droplets coalesce and grow heavy enough to fall. Requires continued cooling and condensation. Three types by mechanism: convectional (equatorial), orographic (windward slopes), and frontal/cyclonic (mid-latitudes).

nodes.label: Convectional Rainfall
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Rainfall caused by intense heating of the surface creating strong convection currents. Hot air rises rapidly, cools, condenses, and produces heavy afternoon thunderstorms. Common in equatorial regions (daily pattern) and continental interiors in summer. Accompanied by thunder and lightning. Localized and intense.

nodes.label: Orographic Rainfall
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Rainfall caused when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier. Windward side receives heavy rainfall as air cools during ascent. Leeward side receives very little rain (rain shadow effect) as descending air warms. Explains why Cherrapunji/Mawsynram receive extreme rainfall while Shillong Plateau is drier.

nodes.label: Frontal/Cyclonic Rainfall
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Rainfall caused when warm air is lifted over cold air at a front. Warm front produces widespread gentle rain over long duration. Cold front produces intense but shorter rainfall along a narrow band. Common in mid-latitudes where polar and tropical air masses meet. Associated with temperate cyclones.

nodes.label: Clouds
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Visible mass of water droplets or ice crystals suspended in the atmosphere. Classified by altitude: high (cirrus, cirrostratus, cirrocumulus above 6000m), middle (altostratus, altocumulus 2000-6000m), low (stratus, stratocumulus, nimbostratus below 2000m). Cumulonimbus extends through all levels. Cloud type indicates weather conditions.

nodes.label: Cirrus Clouds
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: High-altitude clouds above 6000m made of ice crystals. Thin, wispy, feathery appearance. Do not produce precipitation. Indicate fair weather but approaching warm front when thickening. Cirrostratus creates a halo around sun/moon. Most common cloud type in the atmosphere.

nodes.label: Cumulonimbus Clouds
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Towering vertical clouds extending from low levels to the tropopause (up to 15 km). Produce thunderstorms, heavy rain, hail, lightning, and sometimes tornadoes. Flat anvil-shaped top where rising air hits the tropopause. Associated with convectional and frontal rainfall. Most dramatic and dangerous cloud type.

nodes.label: Fog and Mist
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Cloud at ground level formed by condensation near the surface. Fog reduces visibility below 1 km; mist reduces it to 1-2 km. Types: radiation fog (clear nights, calm conditions), advection fog (warm air over cold surface), upslope fog, and steam fog (cold air over warm water). Common in winter in northern India.

nodes.label: Dew and Frost
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Dew is water droplets deposited on cool surfaces when temperature drops to dew point. Forms on clear, calm nights. Frost forms when the dew point is below 0C, causing water vapour to deposit directly as ice crystals (sublimation). White frost damages crops in winter. Both are forms of condensation on surfaces.

nodes.label: Hydrological Cycle
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Continuous circulation of water between earth's surface and atmosphere. Evaporation from oceans and land, transpiration from plants, condensation forming clouds, precipitation as rain/snow, runoff through rivers, infiltration into groundwater, and back to oceans. Driven by solar energy and gravity. Maintains earth's water balance.

nodes.label: Rain Shadow Effect
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Dry area on the leeward side of a mountain that receives significantly less rainfall than the windward side. Air descends on the leeward side, warming adiabatically and reducing relative humidity. Examples: eastern slopes of Western Ghats, Patagonia east of Andes, Great Basin east of Sierra Nevada.

nodes.label: Greenhouse Gases
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Gases that trap infrared radiation in the atmosphere causing warming. Include carbon dioxide (CO2, from fossil fuels), methane (CH4, from agriculture and wetlands), nitrous oxide (N2O), CFCs, and water vapour. CO2 is most significant by volume but methane has 25x higher warming potential per molecule. Concentrations rising since Industrial Revolution.

nodes.label: Montreal Protocol
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: International treaty signed in 1987 to phase out production of ozone-depleting substances, primarily CFCs. Most successful international environmental agreement. Ratified by all UN member states. Led to significant recovery of the ozone layer. Kigali Amendment (2016) added HFCs (potent greenhouse gases) to phase-down list.

nodes.label: IPCC
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, established in 1988 by WMO and UNEP. Assesses scientific knowledge on climate change, its impacts, and mitigation options. Produces comprehensive Assessment Reports. Shared Nobel Peace Prize in 2007 with Al Gore. Key body informing international climate negotiations.

nodes.label: UNFCCC and Paris Agreement
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (1992) is the parent treaty for global climate action. Kyoto Protocol (1997) set binding emission targets for developed nations. Paris Agreement (2015) aims to limit warming to 1.5-2C above pre-industrial levels through nationally determined contributions (NDCs) by all countries.

nodes.label: Ocean Waves
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Oscillatory movement of water surface caused primarily by wind. Water particles move in circular orbits but don't travel with the wave (energy moves, not water). Wave height depends on wind speed, duration, and fetch (distance over water). Waves erode coastlines, transport sediment, and shape coastal landforms.

nodes.label: Tsunami
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Series of ocean waves caused by underwater earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, or landslides. Travel at speeds up to 800 km/h in deep ocean but are barely noticeable. Wave height increases dramatically in shallow coastal water. 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed over 230,000 people. Early warning systems now operational.

nodes.label: Genetic Diversity
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Variation of genes within a species. Enables populations to adapt to changing environments. Greater genetic diversity means more resilience to diseases and environmental changes. Rice varieties in India range from 50,000 to 200,000. Loss of genetic diversity makes species vulnerable to extinction.

nodes.label: Species Diversity
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Variety of species found in a given area. Measured by species richness (number of species) and relative abundance. Highest in tropical regions, decreases toward poles (latitudinal gradient). Coral reefs, tropical rainforests, and deep sea are most species-rich ecosystems. India has about 45,000 plant and 91,000 animal species.

nodes.label: Biodiversity Hotspot
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Region with at least 1,500 endemic plant species and having lost 70% or more of its original habitat. Concept by Norman Myers. Currently 36 recognized hotspots worldwide covering only 2.5% of land but containing 50% of endemic plant species. India has 4 hotspots: Western Ghats, Himalayas, Indo-Burma, and Sundaland.

nodes.label: Endemic Species
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Species found exclusively in a particular geographic area and nowhere else. Islands and isolated habitats have high endemism. Western Ghats has many endemic amphibians and plants. Nilgiri tahr, lion-tailed macaque are endemic to Western Ghats. Endemism is a key criterion for biodiversity hotspot designation.

nodes.label: Ex-situ Conservation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Conservation of species outside their natural habitats. Includes zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, gene banks, captive breeding programs, and cryopreservation. Svalbard Global Seed Vault stores crop seeds. Used when in-situ conservation is not feasible. Captive breeding programs have saved species like the California condor.

nodes.label: Invasive Alien Species
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Non-native species introduced into new environments where they outcompete native species. Examples: water hyacinth (Eichhornia) in Indian water bodies, Lantana camara in forests, Prosopis juliflora in arid areas. Cause ecological damage by displacing native species, altering habitats, and disrupting food chains. Major threat to island biodiversity.

nodes.label: Indira Point
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Southernmost point of India located on Great Nicobar Island at 6d45'N latitude. Also known as Pygmalion Point. Submerged during the 2004 tsunami. India's extreme points: Northernmost - near Indira Col (Siachen Glacier, J&K), Easternmost - Kibithu (Arunachal Pradesh), Westernmost - Guhar Moti (Gujarat/Sir Creek area).

nodes.label: River Pollution in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Major rivers severely polluted by untreated sewage, industrial effluents, agricultural runoff, and religious offerings. Yamuna in Delhi, Ganga at Kanpur and Varanasi are critically polluted. National Mission for Clean Ganga (Namami Gange) launched in 2014. Pollution affects drinking water, aquatic life, and downstream agriculture.

nodes.label: Retreating Monsoon (Oct-Nov)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Withdrawal of southwest monsoon from northwest India from September, completing by December. Characterized by clear skies and high temperatures (October heat). Northeast monsoon brings rainfall to Tamil Nadu coast (Coromandel coast) from Bay of Bengal. Tropical cyclones form in Bay of Bengal during this period, hitting eastern coast.

nodes.label: Northeast Monsoon
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Winter monsoon blowing from land to sea (northeast to southwest) during October-December. Generally dry but picks up moisture while crossing Bay of Bengal and brings significant rainfall to Tamil Nadu and southern AP coast (Coromandel coast). Chennai receives most of its annual rainfall during this period. Associated with cyclonic activity.

nodes.label: India's Rainfall Distribution
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Highly uneven: from 11,871mm at Mawsynram to <100mm in western Rajasthan. Western Ghats windward side, northeast India, and Himalayan foothills receive heaviest rainfall. Leeward side of Western Ghats, western Rajasthan, and interior Deccan are rain shadow areas. Average annual rainfall: about 1,150mm. 80% from southwest monsoon.

nodes.label: Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Irregular oscillation of sea surface temperatures in the Indian Ocean. Positive IOD: western Indian Ocean warmer, eastern cooler - generally enhances Indian monsoon rainfall. Negative IOD: eastern warmer, western cooler - may weaken monsoon. Independent of ENSO but can interact with it. Discovered in 1999 by Saji and Yamagata.

nodes.label: Tropical Cyclones in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India is highly vulnerable to tropical cyclones from both Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. Bay of Bengal cyclones are more frequent and intense. Peak season: October-November (retreating monsoon) and May-June (pre-monsoon). Eastern coast more affected than western. AP, Odisha, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal most vulnerable. IMD monitors and predicts cyclones.

nodes.label: India's Natural Vegetation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India's vegetation is highly diverse due to varied climate, topography, and soil. Classified into five major types: tropical evergreen, tropical deciduous, tropical thorn, montane, and littoral/swamp. Forest cover: about 24.62% of geographic area (2021). National Forest Policy 1988 aims for 33% cover. Vegetation distribution primarily determined by rainfall.

nodes.label: Medicinal Plants
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India has about 8,000 species of medicinal plants. Traditional systems (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani) use many native plants. Important species: neem, tulsi, ashwagandha, brahmi, cinchona (quinine), taxus (cancer treatment), Rauwolfia (blood pressure). Western Ghats and northeast India are richest zones. Over-exploitation is a threat.

nodes.label: Champion and Seth Classification
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: H.G. Champion and S.K. Seth classified India's forests into 16 major types based on temperature, rainfall, and soil. Major groups: tropical forests (wet evergreen to thorn), montane subtropical, montane temperate, sub-alpine, alpine, and littoral/swamp forests. Most widely used classification for Indian forests.

nodes.label: Project Tiger
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Launched in 1973 to protect the Bengal tiger and its habitat. Initially 9 tiger reserves, now 54. NTCA (National Tiger Conservation Authority) manages it. Tiger census uses camera trapping. Tiger population increased from 1,411 (2006) to 3,167+ (2022). Core-buffer strategy. Jim Corbett was the first tiger reserve. India has 75% of world's wild tigers.

nodes.label: Soil Profile
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Vertical cross-section of soil from surface to parent rock showing distinct layers (horizons). O horizon: organic matter. A horizon: topsoil with humus (zone of eluviation). B horizon: subsoil enriched with minerals from above (zone of illuviation). C horizon: weathered parent rock. Mature soils have all horizons; immature soils may lack some.

nodes.label: Soil Conservation in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Methods to prevent soil erosion and maintain soil fertility. Contour ploughing (along contours, not slopes), terrace farming (in hills), strip cropping (alternate strips of different crops), windbreaks/shelter belts (trees against wind erosion), crop rotation, mulching, and afforestation. Contour bunding used on sloped land.

nodes.label: Soil Degradation
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Decline in soil quality due to erosion, salinization, waterlogging, chemical contamination, or loss of organic matter. About 130 million hectares in India affected. Causes: deforestation, overgrazing, improper irrigation, excessive use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides. Gully and ravine erosion prominent in Chambal region.

nodes.label: Humus
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Organic component of soil formed by decomposition of plant and animal matter. Dark brown or black in color. Improves soil structure, water retention, and nutrient content. Highest in forest soils and peaty soils. Lowest in desert and laterite soils. Critical for soil fertility. Can be enriched through composting and organic farming.

nodes.label: Natural Hazard
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Natural event with potential to cause harm to life, property, and environment. Becomes a disaster when it impacts a vulnerable population. Types: geological (earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, landslides, tsunamis), climatic (cyclones, floods, droughts, heatwaves), and biological (epidemics). India is vulnerable to multiple hazards simultaneously.

nodes.label: Earthquakes in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India divided into 4 seismic zones (II-V, V being most severe). Zone V includes Kashmir, NE India, Kutch, Andaman-Nicobar. Zone IV includes Delhi, northern UP, Bihar. Most earthquakes caused by Indian plate pushing into Eurasian plate. Major earthquakes: Bhuj 2001 (7.7), Kashmir 2005 (7.6), Nepal 2015 (7.8). IS 1893 governs earthquake-resistant construction.

nodes.label: Floods in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India's most frequent natural disaster. About 40 million hectares flood-prone. Causes: heavy monsoon rainfall, poor drainage, deforestation, encroachment of floodplains. Most affected: Brahmaputra and Ganga basins (Assam, Bihar, UP, Bengal). Flash floods in Himalayan rivers. Flood management through dams, embankments, channel improvement, and watershed management.

nodes.label: Drought in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Prolonged period of deficient rainfall leading to water scarcity, crop failure, and famine. Types: meteorological (rainfall deficiency), hydrological (water availability), agricultural (soil moisture). Chronic drought areas: Rajasthan, Gujarat, central Maharashtra, Karnataka, AP. Linked to El Nino weakening the monsoon. About 68% of cropped area is drought-prone.

nodes.label: Landslides
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Mass movement of rock, debris, or soil down a slope. Common in Himalayas, Western Ghats, and Nilgiris. Triggered by heavy rainfall, earthquakes, deforestation, road construction. Most vulnerable areas: Northeast India, Himalayan states (J&K, HP, Uttarakhand, Sikkim), and Western Ghats. Flash floods often triggered by landslide dams.

nodes.label: Cyclone Disaster in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India experiences 5-6 tropical cyclones annually, of which 2-3 are severe. Bay of Bengal cyclones are more destructive than Arabian Sea ones. Major impacts: storm surge (most deadly), high winds, heavy rainfall, flooding. Super Cyclone 1999 (Odisha), Cyclone Phailin 2013, Cyclone Amphan 2020, Cyclone Biparjoy 2023. NDMA coordinates disaster response.

nodes.label: Tsunami in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami (caused by 9.1 magnitude earthquake off Sumatra) was the deadliest natural disaster in Indian Ocean history. Over 230,000 killed across 14 countries. India: 16,000+ deaths (Tamil Nadu, Andaman, Pondicherry, Kerala, AP). Led to Indian Tsunami Early Warning System at INCOIS, Hyderabad. Heightened coastal disaster preparedness.

nodes.label: Disaster Management in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Disaster Management Act 2005 established NDMA (chaired by PM), SDMA (state level), DDMA (district level). Shift from relief-centric to preparedness approach. Sendai Framework (2015-2030) guides global disaster risk reduction. National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) for immediate response. Mitigation, preparedness, response, and recovery are four phases.

nodes.label: NDMA
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: National Disaster Management Authority, apex body for disaster management in India. Established under Disaster Management Act 2005. Chaired by the Prime Minister. Responsible for policies, plans, and guidelines for disaster management. Coordinates response to major disasters. Oversees National Disaster Response Force (NDRF).

nodes.label: Volcanic Activity in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India has limited volcanic activity. Barren Island (Andaman) is the only active volcano. Narcondam Island (Andaman) is dormant. Deccan Traps are evidence of massive ancient volcanism (66 mya). India is not on an active plate boundary for volcanism. Nearby volcanic arc (Sunda Trench) poses indirect risks through tsunamis.

nodes.label: Heatwave
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Period of abnormally high temperatures exceeding normal by 4.5-6.4C. Severe heatwave when departure exceeds 6.4C. Common in northern and central India (March-June). Rising frequency due to climate change. Causes heatstroke, crop damage, water scarcity, and power shortages. 2015 heatwave killed over 2,500 people. IMD issues heatwave warnings.

nodes.label: Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Sudden release of water from a glacial lake when the moraine dam breaches due to melting. Causes devastating flash floods downstream. Increasing risk due to global warming melting Himalayan glaciers. Kedarnath disaster (2013) partly attributed to glacial lake burst and cloudburst. Uttarakhand, Sikkim, and Arunachal Pradesh most vulnerable.

nodes.label: Cloudburst
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Sudden, intense rainfall (>100mm per hour) over a small area. Common in hilly regions, especially Himalayas. Causes flash floods, landslides, and debris flows. Orographic lifting combined with convective activity triggers cloudbursts. Kedarnath (2013), Leh (2010) are notable examples. Difficult to predict due to localized nature.

nodes.label: Storm Surge
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Abnormal rise in sea level caused by cyclonic winds pushing water toward the coast. Most deadly aspect of tropical cyclones - causes majority of cyclone fatalities. Height can exceed 5-6 meters in severe cyclones. Low-lying coastal areas most vulnerable (Sundarbans, Andhra Pradesh coast, Odisha). Exacerbated by high tide and sea-level rise.

nodes.label: Seismic Zones of India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India divided into 4 seismic zones (Zone II to V). Zone V (very high risk): Kashmir, western Himalayas, NE India, Kutch, Andaman-Nicobar. Zone IV (high risk): northern plains, Delhi, central Himalayas. Zone III (moderate): parts of peninsular India, Maharashtra. Zone II (low risk): stable peninsular shield. 59% of India is seismically vulnerable.

nodes.label: Flood Management
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Structural measures: dams, embankments, channel improvement, drainage improvement, diversion floodways. Non-structural: flood forecasting (CWC), flood plain zoning, flood insurance, watershed management, afforestation. India has Flood Forecasting Network with 325+ stations. Kosi, Brahmaputra, and Ganga systems have major flood control infrastructure.

nodes.label: Sendai Framework for DRR
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: International agreement adopted in 2015 at Sendai, Japan for disaster risk reduction (2015-2030). Successor to Hyogo Framework. Four priorities: understanding disaster risk, strengthening governance, investing in resilience, and enhancing preparedness. Seven global targets including reducing disaster mortality and economic losses. India actively participates.

nodes.label: Vulnerability and Risk
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Vulnerability is the susceptibility of a community to a hazard. Risk = Hazard x Vulnerability / Capacity. Factors: poverty, population density, poor infrastructure, location, lack of awareness. Reducing vulnerability through preparedness, building codes, early warning systems, and community awareness reduces disaster risk even if hazards cannot be prevented.

nodes.label: Population Distribution in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India's population is unevenly distributed, with about 76% concentrated in 10 states including UP, Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal. Distribution influenced by physical (climate, terrain, water), socio-economic (agriculture, transport, urbanisation) and historical factors.
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: Population Density
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Expressed as persons per sq km. India's density was 313 persons/sq km in 2001, ranking third in Asia after Bangladesh (849) and Japan (334). Ranges from 13 in Arunachal Pradesh to 9,340 in Delhi NCT.
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: Physiological Density
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Total population divided by net cultivated area. Gives better insight into human-land ratio in terms of pressure on cultivable land. More relevant for agrarian countries like India.
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: Agricultural Density
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Total agricultural population (cultivators, agricultural labourers and families) divided by net cultivable area. Significant for understanding pressure on agricultural land.
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: Decadal Growth Rate
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Percentage change in population over a decade. India's growth rate was 21.54% during 1991-2001. Kerala registered lowest (9.4%), while NE states and some UTs recorded very high rates.
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: Adolescent Population
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Age group 10-19 constitutes about 22% of India's population (2001). Male adolescents 53%, female 47%. Challenges include low age at marriage, illiteracy, school dropouts, high maternal mortality.
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: National Youth Policy 2003
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Launched in 2003 by Government of India for all-round improvement of youth and adolescents. Focuses on youth empowerment, women and girl child empowerment, health, sports, and patriotism.
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: Linguistic Composition of India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 179 languages and 544 dialects (Grierson survey). Four language families: Indo-European (73%), Dravidian (20%), Austric (1.38%), Sino-Tibetan (0.85%). Hindi speakers form 40.42%.
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: Religious Composition of India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Hindus 80.5%, Muslims 13.5%, Christians 2.3%, Sikhs 1.9%, Buddhists 0.9%, Jains 0.4% (2001). Spatial distribution varies, with Muslims concentrated in J&K, parts of WB, Kerala, UP.
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: Working Population Composition
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Population divided into main workers (183+ days), marginal workers (<183 days) and non-workers. Only 39% are workers (2001), 61% non-workers. Work participation ranges from 25% (Goa) to 53% (Mizoram).
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: Occupational Structure
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 58.2% in primary sector (cultivators and agricultural labourers), 4.2% in household industries, 37.6% in other workers. Share of agriculture declining (66.85% in 1991 to 58.2% in 2001), indicating sectoral shift.
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: North Indian Plains
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Major concentration zone for India's population due to fertile alluvial soils, water availability, and long history of settled agriculture. Includes Ganga plains, deltas, and coastal plains.
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: Census of India 2001
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Recorded India's population at 1,028 million. Classified workers into cultivators, agricultural labourers, household industrial workers, and other workers. Provided comprehensive demographic data.
nodes.chapter_title: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition

nodes.label: Migration in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 30% of population (307 million) were migrants by place of birth in 2001. Migration integral to population redistribution. India witnessed waves of migrants from Central/West Asia and Southeast Asia historically.

nodes.label: International Migration
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Over 5 million immigrants to India (2001), 96% from neighbours: Bangladesh (3M), Pakistan (0.9M), Nepal (0.5M). Indian diaspora of 20 million across 110 countries.

nodes.label: Remittances
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India received US$11 billion from international migrants in 2002. Punjab, Kerala and Tamil Nadu receive significant amounts. Used for food, debt repayment, education, agriculture, housing.

nodes.label: Consequences of Migration
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Economic: remittances vs overcrowding/slums. Demographic: redistribution, age-sex imbalances. Social: cultural intermixing vs anonymity. Environmental: pressure on infrastructure, pollution.

nodes.label: Slum Formation due to Migration
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Unregulated migration to metropolitan cities causes overcrowding and slum development in industrially developed states like Maharashtra, Gujarat, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Delhi.

nodes.label: Human Development in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: India ranked 127/172 with HDI 0.602 (medium, UNDP 2005). Kerala tops (0.638), Bihar lowest (0.367). Planning Commission prepared India HDR using states as units.

nodes.label: Literacy in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Overall 65.4% (2001), female 54.16%. Kerala highest (90.92%), Bihar lowest (47.53%). Wide regional disparities.

nodes.label: Poverty in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 26.10% below poverty line (1999-2000). Orissa highest (47.15%), Bihar (42.60%). Goa lowest (4.40%).

nodes.label: Social Empowerment
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Freedom from hunger, poverty, ignorance is key. Literacy is beginning of access to knowledge and freedom.

nodes.label: Child Sex Ratio
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 0-6 years ratio declining. Below 800 in Haryana/Punjab. Only Kerala exception. Linked to female foeticide and sex determination.

nodes.label: Female Literacy
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: National 54.16%. Kerala 87.86%, Bihar 33.57%. Literacy gap: Kerala 6.34% vs Bihar 26.75%.

nodes.label: Regional Disparities
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Colonial distortions persist. Government focuses on balanced development through planned development and social distributive justice.

nodes.label: Urban Settlements in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Ancient (Varanasi, Pataliputra), medieval (Delhi, Hyderabad, Jaipur), modern (Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata by British). Post-independence: Chandigarh.

nodes.label: Urbanisation Trends
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 28% in 2001. 11-fold increase in 20th century. 6 mega cities. Greater Mumbai 16.4M. Growth rate slowed in last two decades.

nodes.label: Functional Classification
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Administrative, Industrial, Transport/Port, Commercial, Mining, Educational, Religious, Tourist towns. Cities become multifunctional.

nodes.label: Urban Agglomeration
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Town with outgrowths, contiguous towns, or city with adjoining towns. 35 metropolitan, 6 mega cities. Railway colonies, campuses are outgrowths.

nodes.label: Class-wise Towns
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Census 6 classes. Class I (1 lakh+) 423 cities with 61.48% urban population. 35 metropolitan, 6 mega cities.

nodes.label: Satellite Towns
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Ghaziabad, Rohtak, Gurgaon around Delhi. Urban spillover and increasing rural investment.

nodes.label: Petrochemical Industries
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Polymers, synthetic fibres, elastomers, surfactants. Mumbai hub. IPCL. Cracker units at Auraiya, Jamnagar, Haldia.

nodes.label: IT Industry
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Fastest growing. Exports Rs.78,230 crore (2004-05). 2% GDP. Software parks. MNCs R&D centres. Employment doubles yearly.

nodes.label: LPG Policy 1991
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Abolished licensing (except 6). FDI liberalised. Privatisation. Globalisation. Gap between developed/developing states widening.

nodes.label: Road Transport
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 33.1 lakh km (2005). 85% passengers, 70% freight. NH 2% length but 40% traffic. NHAI 1995. Golden Quadrilateral connects four metros.

nodes.label: Export Composition
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Manufacturing 75.96% (2003-04). Engineering goods growing. Agricultural declining. Petroleum increasing.

nodes.label: Trading Partners
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: USA largest (2004-05). Diversified to EU, China, Japan, UAE. Direction changed from colonial pattern.

nodes.label: Sex Ratio
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: World average 990 females/1000 males. Highest: Latvia (1187). Lowest: UAE (468). Asia generally low. Europe male deficit.

nodes.label: Age-Sex Pyramid
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Expanding (Nigeria wide base), Constant (Australia bell), Declining (Japan narrow base). Shows population characteristics.

nodes.label: World Literacy
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Indicator of socio-economic development. Reveals living standard, female status. India: above 7 years, read/write/arithmetic.

nodes.label: Population Ageing
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Older population share growing. 20th century. Increased life expectancy in developed. Reduced birth rates.

nodes.label: Sex Ratio India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Females per 1000 males. Low in many states. Gender discrimination, female foeticide, domestic violence.

nodes.label: Working Age Group
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 15-59 years. Large working population = productive capacity. Developed have more secondary/tertiary workers.

nodes.label: Dependency Ratio
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Non-working to working population. High young or old increases dependency. Impacts development.

nodes.label: Four Pillars
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Equity (equal access), Sustainability (continuity for future), Productivity (human labour), Empowerment (power to choose).

nodes.label: Approaches to HD
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Income (income=freedom), Welfare (govt expenditure), Basic Needs (ILO), Capability (Amartya Sen).

nodes.label: Amartya Sen Capability
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Increase in freedom as main objective. Social/political institutions increase freedom. Building capabilities.

nodes.label: Mountains
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Natural elevations with small summit and broad base, considerably higher than surroundings. Have permanently frozen rivers of ice called glaciers. Harsh climate, sparse population, limited farming on steep slopes.

nodes.label: Fold Mountains
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Formed by folding of crustal rocks due to compressive forces. Himalayas and Alps are young fold mountains with rugged relief. Aravali is one of the oldest fold mountain systems. Appalachians and Urals are very old.

nodes.label: Block Mountains
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Created when large areas are broken and displaced vertically. Uplifted blocks called horsts, lowered blocks called graben. Rhine valley and Vosges mountain in Europe are examples.

nodes.label: Volcanic Mountains
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Formed due to volcanic activity. Mt. Kilimanjaro in Africa and Mt. Fujiyama in Japan are examples. Built up from accumulation of lava and volcanic material.

nodes.label: Plains
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Large stretches of flat land generally not more than 200m above sea level. Formed by rivers and tributaries depositing stones, sand and silt. Very fertile, thickly populated. Indo-Gangetic plains are most densely populated in India.

nodes.label: Glaciers
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Permanently frozen rivers of ice found in mountains. Source of many rivers. Reservoirs used for irrigation and hydroelectricity generation.

nodes.label: Himalayas
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Young fold mountain range in Asia. Contains world's highest peaks. Storehouse of water through glaciers. Source of major rivers. Rich variety of flora and fauna.

nodes.label: Indo-Gangetic Plains
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Formed by rivers Ganga and Brahmaputra in India. Among the largest river plains in Asia. Extremely fertile alluvial soil. Most densely populated region of India.

nodes.label: River Landforms
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Rivers create waterfalls, meanders, ox-bow lakes, flood plains with levees, and deltas. Erosional features in upper course, depositional features in lower course.

nodes.label: Sea Wave Features
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Erosion creates sea caves, sea arches and stacks from rocky coast. Sea cliffs are steep rocky coasts. Deposition forms beaches along shores.

nodes.label: Glacial Features
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Glaciers erode landscape creating deep hollows that become lakes when ice melts. Deposited material forms glacial moraines.

nodes.label: Wind Landforms
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: In deserts, wind erodes lower sections of rocks more than upper creating mushroom rocks. Sand deposited as sand dunes. Fine sand deposits over large areas called loess (large deposits in China).

nodes.label: Flood Plain
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Flat fertile area formed when river overflows banks and deposits layers of fine soil (sediments). Raised banks called levees. Very fertile for agriculture.

nodes.label: Water Distribution
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Oceans 97.3%, ice caps 2%, ground water 0.68%, fresh water lakes 0.009%, rivers 0.0001%. Despite three-fourths surface covered by water, fresh water is scarce.

nodes.label: Ocean Currents
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Streams of water flowing constantly on ocean surface in definite directions. Warm currents from equator to poles, cold currents from poles to equator. Where they meet: best fishing grounds and foggy weather.

nodes.label: Salinity
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Amount of salt in grams per 1000 grams of water. Average ocean salinity is 35 parts per thousand. Dead Sea has 340g per litre - swimmers float due to high density.

nodes.label: Warm Ocean Currents
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Originate near equator and move towards poles. Gulf Stream is a warm current. Bring warm temperatures to coastal land areas.

nodes.label: Cold Ocean Currents
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Carry water from polar/higher latitudes to tropical/lower latitudes. Labrador current is a cold current. Where warm and cold currents meet, conditions are ideal for fishing.

nodes.label: World Water Day
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Celebrated on March 22 every year to reinforce the need for water conservation. Fresh water is precious and scarce resource.

nodes.label: Human Resources
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: People themselves as a special resource. Knowledge, skill and technology enable best use of nature. Human resource development means improving quality of people's skills through education and health.

nodes.label: Land Use
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Land used for agriculture, forestry, mining, housing, roads, industries. Determined by physical factors (topography, soil, climate, minerals, water) and human factors (population, technology). 90% world population occupies 30% land.
nodes.chapter_title: Land, Soil, Water, Natural Vegetation and Wildlife Resources

nodes.label: Private and Community Land
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Private land owned by individuals. Community land (common property resources) owned by community for common uses: fodder, fruits, nuts, medicinal herbs. Encroachment reducing common lands.
nodes.chapter_title: Land, Soil, Water, Natural Vegetation and Wildlife Resources

nodes.label: Petroleum
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Found between layers of rocks, drilled from offshore and coastal areas. Products: diesel, petrol, kerosene, wax, plastics. Called Black Gold. Producers: Iran, Iraq, Saudi Arabia. India: Digboi (Assam), Bombay High (Mumbai).

nodes.label: Agriculture
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Primary activity including growing crops, fruits, vegetables, flowers and rearing livestock. 50% of world's people engaged in it. Two-thirds of India's population dependent. Latin: ager (soil) + culture (cultivation).

nodes.label: Millets
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Coarse grains that grow on less fertile sandy soils. Hardy crop needing low rainfall and moderate temperature. Jowar, bajra, ragi grown in India. Also Nigeria, China, Niger.

nodes.label: Food Security
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Exists when all people at all times have access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food for active healthy life. Agricultural development aims to increase food security by improving farm production.

nodes.label: Farm System
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Agriculture as a system with inputs (seeds, fertilisers, machinery, labour), processes (ploughing, sowing, irrigation, weeding, harvesting) and outputs (crops, wool, dairy, poultry products).

nodes.label: Silicon Valley
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Part of Santa Clara Valley, California near Rocky Mountains. Close to advanced scientific centres. Pleasant climate, good roads and airports. Major hub of world IT industry.

nodes.label: Bengaluru (Silicon Plateau)
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Located on Deccan Plateau, hence Silicon Plateau. Mild climate year-round. Karnataka first to announce IT Policy (1992). Largest availability of skilled managers. Largest number of IT colleges in India.

nodes.label: Population Distribution
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 90% of world population lives on 30% of land. Crowded: S/SE Asia, Europe, NE North America. Sparse: high latitudes, tropical deserts, high mountains, equatorial forests. 60% live in just 10 countries. Three-quarters in Asia and Africa.

nodes.label: Factors Affecting Population Distribution
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Geographical: topography (plains preferred), climate (extremes avoided), soil (fertile plains), water (river valleys dense), minerals (attract settlement). Social: education, health. Cultural: religious significance. Economic: industrial areas.

nodes.label: Population Composition
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Structure of population by age, sex, literacy, health, occupation, income. Population pyramid (age-sex pyramid) shows total population divided into age groups and percentage of males/females in each group.

nodes.label: Life Expectancy
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Number of years an average person can expect to live. Indicator of health and development. Has increased globally due to better medicine and nutrition.

nodes.label: Human Resource Development
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Improving quality of people's skills through education and health so they can create more resources. Ministry of HRD created in India in 1985. Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana started in 2015.

nodes.label: Western Ghats
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Continuous chain except at passes: Thal Ghat, Bhor Ghat, Pal Ghat. Average height 900-1600m. Higher than Eastern Ghats. Cause orographic rainfall on western coast. Peaks: Anai Mudi, Dodda Betta.

nodes.label: India's Biodiversity
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: About 47000 plant species (10th in world). 89000 animal species. 1200 bird species, 2500 fish species. 12 mega-biodiversity countries. Hotspots: Western Ghats, NE India. Endemic species found nowhere else.

nodes.label: India's Biosphere Reserves
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 18 biosphere reserves in India. Include: Sundarbans, Nanda Devi, Nilgiri, Nokrek, Manas, Pachmarhi, Simlipal, Gulf of Mannar, Great Nicobar. Some recognized by UNESCO.

nodes.label: India's Population
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Second most populous country (1.21 billion, Census 2011). 17.5% of world population on 2.4% of land. UP most populous state. Average density 382 persons/sq km. Sex ratio 940 females per 1000 males (2011).

nodes.label: India's Population Distribution
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Uneven distribution due to terrain, climate, water, soil, minerals. Dense: plains (UP, Bihar, WB). Moderate: plateau regions. Sparse: mountains (Arunachal), desert (Rajasthan), dense forests. Five states (UP, MH, Bihar, WB, AP) hold about half.

nodes.label: Population Policy
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: National Population Policy 2000 aims at sustainable development. Focus on adolescent healthcare, family planning, reducing IMR and maternal mortality. NPP targeted to stabilize population by 2045.

nodes.label: India's Literacy
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: Literacy rate 74% (Census 2011). Males 82.1%, females 65.5%. Kerala highest (93.9%), Bihar lowest (63.8%). Literacy gap between males and females narrowing but persists. Key indicator of development.

nodes.label: Sex Ratio in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 940 females per 1000 males (2011). Kerala highest (1084), Haryana lowest (879). Unfavourable due to female foeticide, neglect, domestic violence. Improving slowly. Sex ratio at birth critical indicator.

nodes.label: Urbanisation in India
nodes.subject: geography
nodes.detail: 31.16% urban population (2011). Rapid growth of urban areas due to rural-urban migration for employment, education, healthcare. Leads to pressure on infrastructure, slums, pollution.
